messages.author: 5276ff4387de2618
messages.subject: Re: Legend position in plotted images of cardinal example data
parts:
Hi Jian,

Thank you for using Cardinal! Yes, using R's base graphics, adjusting the window size after plotting will move the legend around a bit, but there is no standard behavior for this.

Right now, there are no options in Cardinal for customizing the size or placement of the automatically-generated legends.

However, you can still make some adjustments by changing the canvas size when outputting the plots to files (pdf, jpeg, png, etc.). In the vignettes, all of the plots are output to pdf behind-the-scenes, which is why they may appear slightly different than the default interactive R graphics.

You can try, for example:

pdf(file="myplot.pdf", height=6, width=6)
## insert image() or plot() commands here
dev.off()

and adjusting the height and width until you get desired results.

In the future, I may try adding more options for customizing the legends, but hopefully this suggestion helps for now!

-Kyle

messages.author: 6033d3c0e7d242fa
messages.subject: Re: Legend position in plotted images of cardinal example data
parts:
For the Cardinal plots generated using base graphics, each plot is generated independently regardless of the layout, which is why each subplot has its own colorkey. This is necessary mainly so that selectROI() works properly and easily, as most of the methods that would create a single colorkey for multiple plots require creating additional plotting regions that throws off the coordinate system.

For Cardinal 1.0 classes (MSImageSet), you can switch the plotting engine from base to "lattice" by setting "lattice=TRUE". This will do what you want and automatically have a single colorkey for all plots.

For Cardinal 2.0 classes (MSImagingExperiment), lattice graphics aren't supported, but if you pass a list() of arguments to "colorkey", these arguments will be passed to the legend() function, so you can modify the placement and other legend() parameters. However, there will still be multiple colorkeys.

If you want to create a single colorkey for all plots by yourself using R code, here is some example code that would help you get started:

library(CardinalWorkflows)
data(pig206)
layout(matrix(c(1,2,3,3), nrow=2, ncol=2), widths=c(3,1))
image(pig206, mz=c(563,888), col.regions=gradient.colors(100), colorkey=FALSE)
image(matrix(1:100, nrow=1, ncol=100), col=gradient.colors(100), xaxt='n', yaxt='n')

-Kylie
